THOUGHT: The clinical picture is classic for a pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE)–type cutaneous disorder: childhood onset of coalescing yellowish papules in flexures and progressive, severe skin laxity with thick, leathery folds in neck, axillae, groins and abdomen. Histology demonstrates calcified elastic fiber fragments in the reticular dermis (von Kossa–positive), which is the hallmark of PXE-like elastin mineralization. The coagulation lab abnormalities (reduced factor X activity and mildly prolonged PT) point to impaired gamma‑carboxylation of vitamin K–dependent proteins. Whole-exome sequencing shows compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in GGCX (gamma‑glutamyl carboxylase), the enzyme required to carboxylate vitamin K–dependent proteins including matrix Gla protein (MGP) and blood coagulation factors; loss of GGCX function causes under‑carboxylated MGP with aberrant mineralization of elastic fibers plus reduced activity of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors. A positive family history (affected sister) and onset in childhood fit an autosomal recessive inheritance. Cardiovascular and ocular examinations are currently normal, which can occur early in PXE-like GGCX disease. Taken together the clinical, histopathologic, laboratory and genetic data make GGCX‑related PXE‑like syndrome the most likely diagnosis. Other differential diagnoses that produce skin laxity and/or elastic fiber abnormalities are listed below in order of decreasing likelihood and with reasons they are less likely in this case.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum–like syndrome due to GGCX (gamma‑glutamyl carboxylase) deficiency (PXE-like with vitamin K–dependent coagulation factor deficiency) — most likely (explains skin findings, von Kossa‑positive calcified elastic fibers, low factor X and compound heterozygous GGCX mutations).
2. Classic pseudoxanthoma elasticum (ABCC6-related PXE) — clinically and histologically similar (elastic fiber calcification and papules in flexures) but less likely given the identified GGCX mutations and the coagulation factor abnormality which is characteristic of GGCX deficiency rather than ABCC6 defects.
3. Congenital cutis laxa (autosomal recessive or dominant forms, e.g., ELN, FBLN5 mutations) — presents with generalized skin laxity from childhood and familial occurrence, but histology shows fragmented elastic fibers without the prominent calcification and does not explain the coagulation abnormality.
4. Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (classical/others causing skin hyperextensibility) — can cause early skin changes and family clustering, but typically shows collagen defects (not calcified elastic fibers), joint hypermobility, and lacks the coagulation/elastic fiber calcification pattern seen here.
5. Keutel syndrome (MGP mutation) or other disorders of soft‑tissue calcification — can cause abnormal calcification of connective tissues related to MGP dysfunction, but Keutel syndrome features (cartilage calcification, brachytelephalangia, respiratory and cardiovascular findings) are absent, and the genetic/biochemical findings here specifically implicate GGCX.
ground_truth: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum-like disorder with coagulation deficiency

Case Information:
A Chinese woman in her late 20s presented with a 20-year history of progressive skin laxity. In early childhood, she had developed asymptomatic yellowish coalesced papules confined to flexural areas. Subsequently, severe skin sagging occurred on her abdomen with loss of elasticity, then spread extensively with developmental growth. The patient had no extracutaneous involvement and was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. Her younger sister had developed the same skin symptoms.

Physical Examination:
Thick and leathery skinfolds on the neck, axillae, inguinal regions, abdomen, and limbs, with yellowish papules scattered on the dorsal neck.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory tests:     - Low clotting activity of factor X (52.2%; reference range, 77%-131%)    - Prolonged prothrombin time (12.8 seconds; reference range, 10.4-12.6 seconds)    - Other laboratory investigations were unremarkable      - Imaging studies:    - Echocardiographic examination results were normal    - Fundoscopic examination results were normal  - Histopathology:    Image Title: Skin biopsy specimen from neck    Image Description: Shows excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments scattered in the reticular dermis (von Kossa staining)  - Genetic Testing:    Whole-exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous sequence variation in GGCX gene:    - c.1167_1172delCTGGACinsGGGAA (p. Asn389Lys fs*13) in exon 8     - c.824C>T (p. Ser275Leu) in exon 7

ground_truth_patient_facts: 1. A Chinese woman in her late 20s.
2. She presented with a 20-year history of progressive skin laxity.
3. In early childhood, she had developed asymptomatic yellowish coalesced papules confined to flexural areas.
4. Subsequently, severe skin sagging occurred on her abdomen with loss of elasticity.
5. The severe skin sagging then spread extensively with developmental growth.
6. The patient had no extracutaneous involvement.
7. She was born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents.
8. Her younger sister had developed the same skin symptoms.
ground_truth_exam_facts: 1. Thick and leathery skinfolds were present on the neck, axillae, inguinal regions, abdomen, and limbs.
2. Yellowish papules were scattered on the dorsal neck.
3. Low clotting activity of factor X was 52.2% (reference range, 77%-131%).
4. Prothrombin time was prolonged at 12.8 seconds (reference range, 10.4-12.6 seconds).
8. Skin biopsy specimen from neck shows excessive calcification of elastic fiber fragments scattered in the reticular dermis (von Kossa staining).
9. Whole-exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous sequence variation in GGCX gene.
10. c.1167_1172delCTGGACinsGGGAA (p. Asn389Lys fs*13) was identified in exon 8 of GGCX.
11. c.824C>T (p. Ser275Leu) was identified in exon 7 of GGCX.
